title: Laundromat Machine Count
story: Your laundromat works by reservation. Customers book a washing machine for a window in minutes after opening: [10, 40] means load at minute 10, machine free again at minute 40, ready for a load starting at 40.
Machines are expensive. Given a busy Saturday's reservations, how few machines could have served everyone on time?
task: Write machinesNeeded(loads). Each load is [start, end] with start < end. Return the minimum number of machines so every load runs on some machine and no machine runs two loads at once.
A load ending at time t and one starting at t can share a machine. An empty list needs 0 machines.

examples.explanation: From minute 10 to 40 two loads run at once, so you need at least 2 machines. 2 is enough: machine A runs [0, 45] then [50, 95]; machine B runs [10, 40] then [40, 70].
Each load starts exactly when the previous one ends, so one machine runs all three back to back.

hints: In the first example, pick any minute and count the loads running then. What is the largest count, and how does it relate to the answer?
You can never use fewer machines than the most loads running at once, and you never need more. So: what is the peak number of loads in progress?
The count only changes when a load starts (+1) or ends (-1). Visit those moments in time order and track the count. What should happen when an end and a start share a minute?

Sort the start times, and separately the end times. Walk the starts in order; before counting a start, release every load whose end ≤ that start (one pointer into the sorted ends). Track the running count and its maximum. Ends at the same minute go first, because touching loads can share a machine.
bruteForce: For each load's start time t, scan the whole list to count loads running then (start ≤ t < end). The peak is the answer, because the busiest moment is always some load's start.
That is O(n²), about 100 million comparisons for 10,000 loads, recounting the same loads again and again. Sorting lets you keep a running count instead.

js: * @return {number} fewest machines that serve every load

tests.note: one long load, short ones reuse a second machine
counting everything that overlaps one load gives 5
machines handed over at the same minute

js: const starts = loads.map(l => l[0]).sort((a, b) => a - b);
const ends = loads.map(l => l[1]).sort((a, b) => a - b);
// Free every machine whose load is done by now.
py: starts = sorted(s for s, _ in loads)
ends = sorted(e for _, e in loads)
# Free every machine whose load is done by now.
walkthrough: The answer is the most loads running at the same moment. Fewer machines fail at that moment, and that many always suffice, since each new load can take any free machine. To find the peak, sweep through time: a start adds a running load, an end removes one.
• Start 40. Release the end at 40 first: running 1. Then start: running 2. Peak stays 2.
• Start 50. Release the end at 45: running 1. Start: running 2. Answer: 2.

Releasing ends with ≤ before counting the start lets touching loads share a machine; with < you would report 3. The inner loop never runs past the end of ends: the current load's own end is still waiting, and it is greater than the current start.
solution.timeWhy: Two sorts; the sweep moves each pointer through its list once.
solution.spaceWhy: The two sorted lists of times.
solution.takeaway: To count intervals active at the busiest moment, split them into start and end events, sort, and sweep with a running count. A min-heap of end times does the same job and also tells you which machine to reuse.
